examples.title: A screen that went nowhere
examples.summary: Jayden Daniels completed a pass to Deebo Samuel for no gain.
examples.explanation: Samuel caught the ball 3 yards behind the line and gained 3 after the catch. That only brought Washington back to where it started. FTN charted a screen with motion. Compare this with Cook’s 51-yard screen: the design label does not tell you whether it worked. Watch the receiver’s room after the catch, then check the final spot.

examples.title: Sixteen yards, still short
examples.summary: Jordan Love found Chris Brooks for 16 yards on third-and-19.
examples.explanation: Brooks caught the ball 5 yards behind the line and added 21 after the catch. It was a substantial run with the ball, but Green Bay still faced fourth-and-three. FTN did not chart a screen. A catch behind the line does not establish the design, and a large gain does not necessarily keep the drive alive.

examples.title: The fake is only part of the explanation
examples.summary: Jordan Love completed a 23-yard pass to Luke Musgrave.
examples.explanation: FTN charted motion and play action. The catch supplied all 23 yards; there were none afterward. Those facts identify the run fake and the gain, but not a defender’s reaction. On a replay, follow a defender behind the line through the fake, then look for a receiver entering the space he leaves.

examples.title: The catch left work to do
examples.summary: Lamar Jackson found Tylan Wallace for 10 yards on third-and-seven.
examples.explanation: Wallace caught the ball 3 yards beyond the line, still 4 short of the marker. His 7 yards after the catch turned the completion into a first down. When a throw arrives short, shift your attention to the space in front of the receiver and the first defender who can close it.

examples.title: A sack without extra rushers
examples.summary: Michael Penix Jr. was sacked for a 9-yard loss on third-and-four.
examples.explanation: FTN counted four pass rushers and no blitzers. Tampa Bay got the sack without sending extra rushers. On a replay, compare the rush with the quarterback’s time to throw. These counts do not tell us whether coverage delayed the throw, a blocker lost, or the quarterback held the ball too long.

examples.title: This time, an extra rusher
examples.summary: Jalen Hurts was sacked for an 8-yard loss on second-and-10.
examples.explanation: FTN counted five pass rushers, including one blitzer. That supports describing a blitz on this play. The sack itself would not establish it. Follow the extra rusher and the protection on a replay; these counts do not establish which player, if any, missed an assignment.

practice.question: What kept this third-down play alive?
practice.evidence: Baltimore needed 7 yards. Wallace caught the ball 3 yards beyond the line and finished with 10.

choices.label: The run after the catch reached the marker
They finished short of the marker

practice.explanation: The catch left 4 yards to go. Wallace added 7 after the catch, reaching the marker with 3 yards to spare. The completion needed that run to convert.

practice.question: Is that enough to call this a screen?
practice.evidence: Brooks caught Love’s pass 5 yards behind the line, then gained 21 with the ball. The final gain was 16 yards.

choices.label: Yes, because the catch was behind the line
No, because screens do not gain that much
The catch location alone does not establish it

practice.explanation: A short catch and a long run can happen on several designs. FTN did not chart this play as a screen. To recognize a screen on TV, also watch for blockers moving ahead of the receiver.

practice.question: What can these facts tell us about the defense?
practice.evidence: FTN charted motion and play action on Love’s 23-yard completion to Musgrave. The throw covered all 23 yards.

choices.label: A defender definitely stepped toward the fake
We need the defender’s reaction to judge the fake’s effect

practice.explanation: The charting confirms the offensive action, not its effect on a defender. Follow one defender through the exchange on a replay, then check the space behind him. The completion alone does not prove he was fooled.

practice.question: How would you describe the result?
practice.evidence: On third-and-19, Green Bay completed a pass for 16 yards. No penalty or first down was recorded.

choices.label: A big gain that earned another set of downs
Better field position, with a fourth-down decision still ahead
Possession automatically went to the defense

practice.explanation: The gain left fourth-and-three. It changed the field position and the distance for a possible conversion, but did not itself keep the drive going. The next decision still depends on the score, clock and spot.

practice.question: Which conclusion is supported?
practice.evidence: Hurts was sacked for an 8-yard loss. FTN charted five pass rushers, including one blitzer.

choices.label: An extra rusher came; responsibility for the sack is not established
An offensive tackle missed the extra rusher

practice.explanation: The rusher count supports calling it a blitz. It does not identify a missed assignment or establish the coverage. Those need a closer look at the protection and receivers.

practice.question: Why did the yards after the catch produce no net gain?
practice.evidence: Samuel caught a pass 3 yards behind the line and gained 3 after the catch. The play ended where it started.

choices.label: A penalty must have erased the gain
The run only recovered the ground behind the line
It must have been ruled incomplete

practice.explanation: The 3 yards with the ball brought Samuel back to the starting line. After-catch yardage can look productive while the offense gains no ground. On a screen, compare the catch point and final spot.
